## Overview of the Enriched Pathways

In Table 1, we rank the enriched biological pathways on the basis of statistical significance, biological coherence, and disease relevance. Among the most informative signals for arrhythmia are muscle- and cardiomyocyte-related pathways, particularly structural constituent of muscle (Gene Ontology:0008307, P < 2.68 × 10−2) and myofibril assembly (Gene Ontology:0030239, P < 3.52 × 10−3). These enrichments point to abnormalities in sarcomeric organization and contractile architecture. This pattern is broadly consistent with prior literature indicating that disruption of myofibrillar structure and cytoskeletal integrity may alter electrical conduction, mechanochemical coupling, and susceptibility to atrial and ventricular arrhythmias. In parallel, the enrichment of regulation of receptor binding (Gene Ontology:1900120, P < 3.31 × 10−4) suggests altered signaling at the cell surface, a mechanism that may influence ion channel regulation, neurohumoral responses, and excitation-contraction coupling, all of which are central to arrhythmia biology.

Taken together, these findings suggest that both structural organization and cell-surface signaling may contribute to the overall enrichment pattern. Extending beyond these core cardiac themes, several additional pathways support a possible role for inflammation, vesicular trafficking, and membrane remodeling in arrhythmia.

Neutrophil degranulation (Reactome:R-HSA-6798695, P < 5.79 × 10−10), one of the most statistically significant findings with 48 associated proteins, together with specific granule membrane (Gene Ontology:0035579, P < 1.93 × 10−3) and efferocytosis (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes:04148, P < 2.98 × 10−3), is compatible with growing evidence that innate immune activation, release of proteases and inflammatory mediators, and defective clearance of damaged cells may promote fibrosis and electrical instability in the heart. Enrichment of late endosome (Gene Ontology:0005770, P < 7.82 × 10−3) further suggests altered intracellular trafficking, which is relevant because endosomal pathways regulate membrane turnover and localization of ion channels and receptors that shape cardiac excitability. The signal for diseases of glycosylation (Reactome:R-HSA-3781865, P < 1.87 × 10−6) and carboxylic acid binding (Gene Ontology:0031406, P < 5.67 × 10−8) also points to metabolic and post-translational mechanisms. Prior studies have shown that abnormal glycosylation may modify channel gating, membrane expression, and intercellular coupling, thereby increasing arrhythmia risk. Although some tissue- or disease-labeled terms, such as colon goblet cells, skin extracellular matrix, pleural mesothelioma, malaria, and spinal cord injury, are likely less disease-specific, they may still reflect shared underlying themes of extracellular matrix remodeling, inflammatory stress, and altered cellular communication that are increasingly recognized as possible contributors to arrhythmia pathogenesis.

This broader set of enrichments therefore complements the muscle-related signals described above and suggests that the observed pathway landscape may involve both cardiac-intrinsic and systemic biological processes. For clarity, the ranked pathways from each source are summarized below.

## Enriched Pathways Analysis

Building on the overview above, the following sections provide a more detailed discussion of the top enriched pathways.


### Colon; goblet cells[≥Low] (HPA:0130891) 

This pathway label refers to colon goblet cells with low or greater activity, indicating a cell population in the colonic epithelium that produces and secretes mucins and other barrier-forming molecules. Goblet cells are essential for intestinal homeostasis because they generate the mucus layer that separates luminal microorganisms and dietary contents from the epithelial surface, thereby limiting microbial translocation, reducing epithelial injury, and shaping local immune tolerance. Through these functions, goblet cells contribute to preservation of epithelial integrity, regulation of inflammatory signaling, and maintenance of host and microbial metabolic interactions. Although this pathway is anatomically localized to the colon rather than the heart, perturbation of goblet cell abundance or function may still influence systemic physiology through impaired barrier defense, altered intestinal microbiota composition, enhanced inflammatory cytokine release, and changes in microbial metabolites. These systemic consequences are biologically relevant to cardiovascular disorders, including arrhythmia, because chronic inflammation, autonomic imbalance, metabolic dysregulation, and fibrosis-promoting signaling are established contributors to abnormal cardiac impulse generation and conduction.

With this biological context in mind, the currently available evidence should be interpreted cautiously. No pathway-specific publications were provided, so there is no direct citation-based evidence linking the colon goblet cell pathway itself to arrhythmia in the supplied literature. On mechanistic grounds, however, a plausible relationship can be inferred through the intestine-heart axis. Goblet cells maintain the mucus barrier of the colon, and reduced goblet cell function may promote epithelial permeability, microbial product translocation, and persistent systemic inflammation. Systemic inflammatory mediators can alter cardiac ion channel activity, calcium handling, structural remodeling, and fibrotic responses, all of which may increase susceptibility to atrial and ventricular rhythm disturbances. In addition, disruption of goblet cell-dependent barrier homeostasis may reshape microbial metabolism and circulating bioactive metabolites, which can affect autonomic regulation, vascular tone, and myocardial electrophysiology. Therefore, while the present evidence set does not permit a direct literature-supported conclusion, this pathway may be indirectly related to arrhythmia through inflammation-driven and microbiota-mediated mechanisms that influence the arrhythmogenic substrate.

This cautious mechanistic interpretation is further supported by the enrichment results observed in the present analysis. There were 36 arrhythmia-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing colon goblet cells with low or greater activity, providing a biologically informative signal that links epithelial barrier regulation, mucin secretion, microbial containment, inflammatory control, and host-to-microbial metabolic balance to systemic processes relevant to arrhythmia. Although this pathway is localized to the colonic epithelium rather than the myocardium, the enrichment of 36 proteins suggests a measurable systems-level connection in which altered goblet cell function may contribute to arrhythmia through several quantitatively meaningful mechanisms, including increased inflammatory cytokine exposure, impaired barrier defense, altered microbiota-derived metabolite production, autonomic perturbation, and fibrosis-promoting signaling that can disrupt cardiac impulse generation and conduction. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 36 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided here: [Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=6FA17AE3E94B9061).

![PPI Network](imgs/c25d9ad4-301b-433d-a374-1db49c34d1c5.png)

To clarify how this enrichment signal may relate to arrhythmia biology, the significant proteins identified in the functional enrichment analysis are introduced below in a more structured manner. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified several significant proteins. We will introduce them in detail in the following.  
CDH1 is among the most relevant proteins in this list for arrhythmia because perturbation of intercellular adhesion is a central mechanism in cardiac electrical instability. Although the annotation provided emphasizes its role in microbial infection, the core biological function of CDH1 is epithelial adherens junction organization, and cadherin-based adhesion is conceptually important for maintaining tissue architecture, mechano-electrical coupling, and coordinated impulse propagation. In the heart, disruption of adhesion complexes can promote structural remodeling, altered cell-cell coupling, conduction heterogeneity, and arrhythmogenic substrate formation. Thus, even if CDH1 is not a canonical arrhythmia gene in this annotation, its adhesion-related biology makes it mechanistically relevant to arrhythmia, particularly in settings of inflammation, infection, or tissue remodeling that impair junctional integrity.

Closely related to this theme of tissue injury and remodeling, infection-associated mechanisms may also be relevant.  
CXADR stands out as highly relevant to arrhythmia because coxsackievirus infection is a well-established cause of myocarditis, and myocarditis is strongly linked to atrial and ventricular arrhythmias. As the coxsackievirus and adenovirus receptor, CXADR mediates viral entry and therefore may influence susceptibility to infection-driven myocardial inflammation, myocyte injury, and subsequent electrical remodeling. These processes can lead to conduction slowing, triggered activity, scar formation, and malignant ventricular arrhythmias. Accordingly, even though the supplied annotation is framed in terms of microbial infection, the disease connection to arrhythmia is compelling through virus-induced myocardial damage and inflammatory cardiomyopathy.

A related but more structural perspective is provided by extracellular matrix and vascular regulation.  
COL18A1 is potentially relevant to arrhythmia because its anti-angiogenic activity, largely attributable to endostatin-containing domains, may influence myocardial vascular homeostasis, ischemic remodeling, and fibrosis. Impaired angiogenesis and abnormal extracellular matrix signaling can contribute to microvascular insufficiency, chronic myocardial stress, and structural remodeling, all of which are recognized substrates for arrhythmogenesis. Its interactions with VEGFA signaling and integrin-dependent migratory pathways further suggest a role in regulating repair responses after injury. In this context, COL18A1 may not directly control ion channels, but it could shape the structural and vascular environment that predisposes to conduction abnormalities and reentrant arrhythmias.[PubMed:9459295](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9459295) [PubMed:11257123](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11257123) 

Beyond extracellular remodeling, intracellular energetic stability is also likely to be important.  
CHCHD10 is notable because mitochondrial integrity is increasingly recognized as a major determinant of cardiac excitability and arrhythmia susceptibility. Proper mitochondrial cristae organization is essential for oxidative phosphorylation, adenosine triphosphate production, calcium buffering, and reactive oxygen species control. Disturbance of these processes can alter membrane excitability, impair ion pump function, promote afterdepolarizations, and trigger cell injury or fibrotic remodeling. Therefore, although the provided annotation is concise, CHCHD10 has a biologically plausible connection to arrhythmia through mitochondrial dysfunction, a mechanism that is particularly relevant in cardiomyopathies and stress-induced electrical instability.

This focus on remodeling can be extended to multifunctional surface proteins involved in tissue interaction networks.  
BSG is not a classical arrhythmia gene, but it is potentially relevant because it is a multifunctional cell-surface glycoprotein involved in adhesion, survival signaling, and tissue interaction networks. More broadly, basigin and cluster of differentiation 147 have established roles in extracellular matrix remodeling and inflammatory signaling in other contexts, which are processes tightly linked to atrial and ventricular arrhythmogenesis. The annotation here emphasizes neural biology, but autonomic regulation is a major modulator of cardiac rhythm, and proteins involved in neuron-cell interactions may influence neurocardiac signaling. In addition, adhesion and remodeling pathways can affect myocardial substrate formation. Thus, BSG is a plausible indirect contributor to arrhythmia susceptibility, especially in inflammatory or remodeling-associated disease states.[PubMed:12089450](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12089450) [PubMed:27922006](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27922006) [PubMed:7533044](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7533044) [PubMed:10625334](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10625334) [PubMed:7516497](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7516497) [PubMed:9262180](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9262180) [PubMed:9469574](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9469574) [PubMed:9482781](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9482781) [PubMed:9482783](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9482783) [PubMed:26335717](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26335717) [PubMed:15953602](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15953602) [PubMed:19158290](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19158290) [PubMed:17640868](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17640868) 

Among the proteins listed, inflammatory and fibrotic mediators may be especially informative for arrhythmogenic remodeling.  
LGALS3 is one of the strongest candidates for arrhythmia relevance in this list because galectin-3 is widely implicated in cardiac inflammation and fibrosis, both of which are major drivers of arrhythmogenic remodeling. The annotated functions support this interpretation: LGALS3 promotes inflammatory cell recruitment and activation, coordinates responses to cellular damage, and participates in tissue remodeling programs. In the heart, these processes can foster fibroblast activation, extracellular matrix deposition, conduction heterogeneity, and atrial or ventricular substrate formation. Consequently, LGALS3 is especially important in fibrotic arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation and in arrhythmias associated with heart failure or inflammatory cardiomyopathy.

Inflammation-related mechanisms may also intersect with metabolic and iron-dependent stress responses.  
LCN2 is potentially important for arrhythmia because dysregulated iron handling, inflammation, and apoptosis can all contribute to myocardial injury and electrical remodeling. The annotation indicates that LCN2 directly influences intracellular iron balance and can induce apoptosis under iron-depleted conditions through BCL2L11 and BIM. In the cardiovascular system, altered iron homeostasis and inflammatory stress may impair mitochondrial function, enhance oxidative stress, and promote fibrosis or myocyte death, thereby creating a substrate for arrhythmia. Its role in innate immunity further strengthens the link to inflammatory arrhythmogenic states, including myocarditis and systemic inflammatory disease.[PubMed:12453413](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12453413) [PubMed:15531878](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15531878) [PubMed:16446425](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16446425) 

In a similar way, proteolytic and lysosomal pathways may contribute indirectly to disease progression.  
LGMN may be relevant to arrhythmia primarily through inflammatory and remodeling pathways. Its role in antigen presentation suggests potential involvement in immune activation, while its functions in lysosomal degradation and epidermal growth factor receptor turnover indicate broader effects on proteostasis and proliferative signaling. In the myocardium, chronic inflammation and altered growth factor signaling can promote fibrosis, hypertrophy, and structural remodeling, all of which facilitate arrhythmia. Although the annotation does not describe a direct electrophysiological role, LGMN could contribute indirectly by shaping inflammatory responses and cellular turnover in diseased cardiac tissue.[PubMed:23776206](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23776206) [PubMed:9872320](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9872320) 

Neurocardiac organization represents another potentially relevant dimension of the enrichment profile.  
NFASC is of interest because ankyrin-associated adhesion systems are fundamental organizers of excitable membrane domains. Although the supplied annotation focuses on neural development and neuron-glial interactions, the ankyrin-binding property is particularly noteworthy in the context of arrhythmia, since ankyrin-based scaffolding is critical for localization of ion channels and membrane proteins in electrically active cells. Disruption of such scaffolding mechanisms can impair excitability and conduction. In addition, autonomic neural regulation strongly influences heart rhythm, so proteins involved in axonal organization and synaptic function may have indirect relevance to arrhythmia through neurocardiac pathways.

This neurohumoral perspective also aligns with broader systemic stress signaling.  
GDF15-related signaling is relevant to arrhythmia in an indirect but potentially important manner because it is a stress-responsive pathway linked to systemic illness, cancer, drug exposure, and metabolic adaptation. The annotation shows that this pathway is activated by diverse stressors and engages defined brainstem circuits. In clinical settings, elevated GDF15 is often associated with cardiovascular stress, heart failure, and adverse outcomes. Through neurohumoral and metabolic effects, this pathway could modulate autonomic tone, cachexia-related frailty, and disease severity, all of which may influence arrhythmia risk. While not a direct electrophysiological effector, it may serve as a marker or mediator of systemic states that predispose to rhythm disturbances.[PubMed:28846097](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846097) [PubMed:28846098](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846098) [PubMed:28846099](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846099) [PubMed:28953886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28953886) [PubMed:31152154](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31152154) [PubMed:31928886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31928886) [PubMed:32723474](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32723474) [PubMed:33593916](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33593916) [PubMed:35202387](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35202387) [PubMed:36630958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36630958) [PubMed:37380764](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37380764) [PubMed:31875646](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31875646) [PubMed:32661391](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32661391) 

At the level of growth control and mechanotransduction, additional indirect links are also plausible.  
YAP1 is a particularly interesting candidate because Hippo-YAP signaling is a major regulator of cell survival, mechanotransduction, regeneration, and fibrosis, all of which are highly relevant to arrhythmogenic remodeling. The annotation specifically links YAP1 to activation of ERBB4 signaling, suggesting participation in growth and stress-response pathways. In cardiac tissue, dysregulated YAP1 activity can influence cardiomyocyte proliferation, fibroblast behavior, and responses to biomechanical stress. These effects may alter myocardial architecture and conduction properties, thereby contributing to arrhythmia susceptibility, especially in structural heart disease.

Finally, cytoskeletal adaptation and injury-response biology may provide an additional layer of indirect relevance.  
GSN may have indirect relevance to arrhythmia through cytoskeletal and injury-response biology, although the provided annotation focuses on stem cell regulation. In a broader mechanistic sense, gelsolin-family functions are connected to actin remodeling, cellular stress responses, and tissue repair. These processes can influence inflammatory remodeling and structural adaptation after cardiac injury. Therefore, while the evidence from the supplied annotation is limited, GSN remains of possible interest as an indirect modulator of the myocardial substrate that supports arrhythmia.[PubMed:7694679](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7694679)
